title: Git Fundamentals for AI-Native Development
description: Git as the versioning substrate for AI-assisted development. Learn branching, commit conventions, recovery techniques, and CI/CD integration through the lens of agent workflows and Paradigm's git-powered features.

lessons.title: Why Git Matters for AI Development
lessons.content:
## Why Git Matters for AI Development

Git is the versioning substrate that makes AI-assisted development safe and auditable. Every change an AI agent makes is tracked, reversible, and attributable. Without version control, letting an agent modify your codebase would be like editing a shared document with no undo history.

### Git as Infrastructure, Not Just a Tool

In traditional development, git is a collaboration tool. In AI-native development, git becomes **infrastructure** — the foundation that other systems build on:

- **Paradigm hooks** run on every commit to enforce `.purpose` file compliance
- **History tracking** parses commit messages to build a timeline of symbol changes
- **Session recovery** uses git state to reconstruct what an agent was working on
- **Review pipelines** use `git diff` to determine what changed and validate it

### How Paradigm Uses Git

Paradigm treats git as a first-class data source:

1. **Post-commit hook**: After every commit, Paradigm parses the `Symbols:` trailer line to record which symbols were touched. This builds a queryable history without manual tracking.

2. **Pre-commit hook**: Before a commit goes through, Paradigm rebuilds its static index (`scan-index.json`) so the index is always in sync with the committed code.

3. **Stop hook**: When an agent session ends, Paradigm checks that `.purpose` files were updated for any modified source directories. If not, the session is blocked until compliance is met.

4. **Git diff in review**: `paradigm review --ci` uses `git diff` to identify changed files and run targeted compliance and quality checks.

### Why Version Control Matters More with AI Agents

Human developers make incremental, deliberate changes. AI agents can modify dozens of files in a single session. This amplifies both the benefit and the risk:

- **Benefit**: An agent can refactor an entire module in seconds, and git captures the full before/after.
- **Risk**: A bad agent session could corrupt many files simultaneously. Git makes this fully reversible with a single `git revert`.

Without git, you would have no way to audit what an agent changed, no way to roll back a bad session, and no way to compare agent A's approach with agent B's approach to the same task.

### The Commit as a Unit of Work

In AI-native development, a commit represents a **completed unit of agent work**. Each commit should be atomic — it either works completely or can be reverted completely. This is why Paradigm encourages agents to commit after finishing a coherent piece of work, not mid-task.

lessons.title: Core Concepts
lessons.content:
## Core Concepts

Git tracks the history of your project as a series of snapshots. Understanding three key areas — the working directory, staging area, and repository — gives you a complete mental model for how changes flow through git.

### The Three Areas

```
Working Directory  -->  Staging Area  -->  Repository
   (your files)        (git add)          (git commit)
```

1. **Working directory**: The files on disk. When an agent edits a file, the change exists only here until staged.

2. **Staging area** (also called the index): A preparation zone. `git add` moves changes here. You can stage some changes and leave others unstaged — this lets you craft focused commits.

3. **Repository**: The permanent history. `git commit` takes everything in the staging area and creates a new snapshot with a unique hash.

### Commits

A commit is a snapshot of every tracked file at a point in time, plus metadata:

- **Hash**: A SHA-1 identifier (e.g., `a1b2c3d`). Immutable — if any bit changes, the hash changes.
- **Parent(s)**: The commit(s) this one was built on. This creates a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
- **Author**: Who made the change.
- **Message**: Why the change was made.

In AI-native workflows, the author is typically the developer, and the commit message often includes a `Co-Authored-By` trailer for the AI agent.

### HEAD and Refs

- **HEAD**: A pointer to your current position in the commit graph. Usually points to a branch name.
- **Branch**: A named pointer to a commit. When you commit, the branch pointer moves forward.
- **Tag**: A named pointer to a commit that does not move. Used for releases.

```
main:      A --- B --- C  <-- HEAD
                  \
 feature:          D --- E
```

In this graph, `main` points to commit C, and `feature` points to commit E. HEAD points to wherever you are currently checked out.

### The Commit Graph

Git's history is a graph, not a line. Every branch creates a fork in the graph. Merges bring forks back together. Understanding this graph is essential for:

- Knowing what a PR contains (commits between branch point and HEAD)
- Understanding what `git log` shows (walking the graph backward from HEAD)
- Resolving merge conflicts (two branches modified the same line divergently)

### Staging for AI Workflows

When an AI agent finishes work, it should stage specific files rather than using `git add .` or `git add -A`. This prevents accidentally committing sensitive files (like `.env`) or build artifacts. Paradigm's conventions explicitly call for adding files by name:

```bash
git add src/auth/login.ts src/auth/.purpose
```

This deliberate staging is a safety practice that becomes critical when agents operate with broad file system access.

HEAD, branches, and the commit graph

lessons.title: Branching for AI Sessions
lessons.content:
## Branching for AI Sessions

Branches are cheap, instant, and essential for safe AI-assisted development. Every AI agent session should work on a branch — never directly on `main`.

### Why Agents Work on Branches

An AI agent session is exploratory by nature. The agent might:

- Take an approach that needs to be discarded
- Make changes that need human review before merging
- Work in parallel with other agents on different tasks

Branches provide isolation. If an agent's work on branch `feat/add-auth` goes wrong, `main` is untouched. You can delete the branch and start over with zero risk.

### Feature Branch Workflow

The standard AI-native workflow:

1. **Create a branch** from `main`:
   ```bash
   git checkout -b feat/add-user-auth
   ```

2. **Agent works** on the branch, making commits as it completes units of work.

3. **Push the branch** to remote:
   ```bash
   git push -u origin feat/add-user-auth
   ```

4. **Open a Pull Request** for human review. The PR shows the full diff between the branch and `main`.

5. **Merge** after review. The branch is deleted.

This workflow ensures that every change to `main` has been reviewed. The branch is the agent's workspace; the PR is the handoff point.

### How `paradigm team` Uses Branches

Paradigm's multi-agent orchestration (`paradigm team orchestrate`) can spawn multiple agents working in parallel. Each agent gets its own branch:

```
main
  |
  +-- agent/architect-auth-design
  +-- agent/builder-auth-impl
  +-- agent/reviewer-auth-review
```

The orchestrator coordinates merges. If agents modify overlapping files, the orchestrator can detect conflicts early through `paradigm_ripple` analysis before branches diverge too far.

### Naming Conventions

Consistent branch names help humans and agents understand what a branch is for:

| Prefix | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|--------|
| `feat/` | New feature | `feat/add-payment-form` |
| `fix/` | Bug fix | `fix/login-redirect-loop` |
| `refactor/` | Code improvement | `refactor/extract-auth-middleware` |
| `agent/` | Agent-managed branch | `agent/builder-auth-impl` |
| `test/` | Test additions | `test/add-checkout-e2e` |

Use kebab-case. Include the primary symbol when relevant: `feat/add-#payment-form` or just `feat/payment-form`.

### Branch Hygiene

After a PR is merged:

- **Delete the remote branch**: Most git hosts do this automatically on merge.
- **Delete the local branch**: `git branch -d feat/add-user-auth`
- **Prune stale remote references**: `git fetch --prune`

Stale branches accumulate fast when agents create branches frequently. Regular cleanup keeps the repository navigable.

lessons.title: Commits Agents Can Parse
lessons.content:
## Commits Agents Can Parse

Commit messages are not just for humans. In Paradigm, commit messages are **machine-readable data** that power history tracking, ripple analysis, and session recovery. Writing structured commits is essential.

### Conventional Commit Format

Paradigm uses a superset of the Conventional Commits standard:

```
type(#primary-symbol): short description

- Detail with #component references
- Gate changes: ^gate-name
- Signals emitted: !signal-name

Symbols: #symbol-a, #symbol-b, !signal-c
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
```

### Breaking It Down

**Subject line**: `type(#symbol): description`

- **type**: The nature of the change — `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`
- **#symbol**: The primary Paradigm symbol affected, in parentheses
- **description**: A concise summary (imperative mood: "add" not "added")

Examples:
```
feat(#payment-form): add Apple Pay support
fix(#auth-middleware): handle expired refresh tokens
refactor(#user-service): extract validation into shared utility
test(#checkout-flow): add integration tests for cart edge cases
```

**Body**: Additional details referencing symbols with their prefixes (`#`, `$`, `^`, `!`, `~`). Each symbol prefix tells you the *kind* of thing being referenced.

**Trailers**: Machine-readable metadata at the end.

### The Symbols Trailer

The `Symbols:` trailer is the most important line for Paradigm:

```
Symbols: #payment-form, #apple-pay-button, $checkout-flow, !payment-method-added
```

Paradigm's **post-commit hook** parses this line and records which symbols were modified in each commit. This powers:

- **`paradigm_history_fragility`**: Shows which symbols change most frequently (fragile symbols need attention)
- **`paradigm_ripple`**: Knows the recent change history of a symbol
- **Session context**: New sessions can see what symbols were recently touched

Without the `Symbols:` trailer, Paradigm must guess from file paths. With it, the connection between commits and symbols is explicit and reliable.

### Rules for Good Agent Commits

1. **One logical change per commit**. Don't bundle a feature, a refactor, and a bug fix.
2. **List ALL affected symbols** in the `Symbols:` trailer — not just the primary one.
3. **Use imperative mood**: "add feature" not "added feature" or "adding feature".
4. **Include the Co-Authored-By trailer** when an AI agent contributed to the work.
5. **Reference gates and signals** in the body when authorization or events change.

### What Agents Parse From Commits

When an agent starts a new session, `paradigm_session_recover` examines recent commits to understand:

- What was the previous agent working on? (subject lines)
- Which symbols are "hot"? (Symbols trailers)
- Are there unfinished flows? (references to `$flow` symbols without completion signals)

This is why commit message quality directly affects the next agent's effectiveness.
keyConcepts: Conventional commit format: type(#symbol): description
The Symbols: trailer enables automatic history tracking
Post-commit hook parses trailers for symbol history
Structured commits improve session recovery for subsequent agents

lessons.title: Recovering from Mistakes
lessons.content:
## Recovering from Mistakes

Mistakes happen — especially when AI agents are making rapid changes across many files. Git provides multiple recovery mechanisms, each suited to different situations.

### git revert: The Safe Undo

`git revert <commit-hash>` creates a **new commit** that undoes the changes from the specified commit. The original commit stays in history.

```bash
git revert a1b2c3d
```

**When to use**: You've already pushed a commit and others may have pulled it. Revert is safe for shared branches because it doesn't rewrite history.

**Agent use case**: An agent's previous session introduced a bug. The new session can `git revert` the bad commit and then fix the issue properly, preserving full traceability.

### git reset: Moving HEAD Backward

`git reset` moves the branch pointer backward. It has three modes:

| Mode | Working Directory | Staging Area | Use Case |
|------|-------------------|-------------|----------|
| `--soft` | Unchanged | Unchanged | Recommit with a better message |
| `--mixed` (default) | Unchanged | Cleared | Unstage changes, keep edits |
| `--hard` | **Cleared** | Cleared | Discard everything |

```bash
# Undo last commit, keep changes staged
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Undo last commit, keep changes unstaged
git reset HEAD~1

# Discard last commit and all changes entirely
git reset --hard HEAD~1
```

**When to use**: The commit hasn't been pushed yet (local only). Reset rewrites history, which causes problems on shared branches.

**Agent use case**: An agent made a commit with the wrong message or included files it shouldn't have. `git reset --soft HEAD~1` lets it redo the commit.

### git stash: Temporary Shelving

`git stash` saves uncommitted changes and reverts your working directory to a clean state.

```bash
# Stash current changes
git stash

# List stashes
git stash list

# Restore most recent stash
git stash pop

# Restore without removing from stash list
git stash apply
```

**When to use**: You need to switch branches but have uncommitted work. Or you want to test something on a clean working directory.

**Agent use case**: An agent needs to check the behavior of `main` before continuing its work. Stash, switch, verify, switch back, pop.

### git reflog: The Ultimate Undo

`git reflog` shows every position HEAD has been at — including commits that are no longer on any branch. It's the ultimate safety net.

```bash
# Show recent HEAD positions
git reflog

# Output:
# a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
# f4e5d6c HEAD@{1}: commit: feat(#auth): add JWT validation
# 9g8h7i6 HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from main to feat/auth
```

Even after a `git reset --hard`, the "lost" commit still exists. You can recover it:

```bash
git checkout f4e5d6c
# or
git reset --hard f4e5d6c
```

Reflog entries expire after 90 days by default. Until then, **nothing is truly lost in git**.

### Session Checkpoints as a Safety Net

Paradigm's `paradigm_session_checkpoint` records the agent's progress at key phases (planning, implementing, validating, complete). If a session crashes:

1. The next agent calls `paradigm_session_recover`
2. The checkpoint shows what was in progress
3. Combined with `git reflog` and `git stash list`, the full state can be reconstructed

This layered approach — git history + reflog + Paradigm checkpoints — means agent work is never truly lost.

### Decision Guide

| Situation | Use |
|-----------|-----------|
| Bad commit already pushed | `git revert` |
| Bad commit not yet pushed | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` |
| Need to temporarily set aside work | `git stash` |
| Accidentally deleted a commit | `git reflog` + `git reset` |
| Agent session crashed mid-work | `paradigm_session_recover` + `git stash list` |
keyConcepts: git revert creates a new commit to undo changes safely
git reset moves HEAD backward (soft, mixed, hard modes)
git reflog is the ultimate safety net — nothing is truly lost
Paradigm session checkpoints complement git recovery

lessons.title: Git in CI/CD
lessons.content:
## Git in CI/CD

Git is not just for local development — it powers the continuous integration and delivery pipeline. In Paradigm, git hooks and the review pipeline work together to enforce quality before code reaches `main`.

### Pre-Commit Hooks

Pre-commit hooks run before a commit is finalized. If the hook exits with a non-zero code, the commit is blocked.

Paradigm installs a pre-commit hook that **rebuilds the static index** (`scan-index.json`) before every commit. This ensures the index is always synchronized with committed code:

```bash
# What the hook does (simplified):
paradigm scan --quiet
git add .paradigm/scan-index.json
```

This is a non-blocking operation — it enhances the commit rather than preventing it.

### Stop Hooks (Session Enforcement)

Paradigm's stop hook runs when an agent session ends. It performs 12 compliance checks:

| Check | What It Validates |
|-------|-------------------|
| 1 | Source files modified without `.purpose` updates |
| 2 | Modified directories missing `.purpose` files |
| 3 | Route patterns added without `portal.yaml` |
| 4 | Aspect anchor files that no longer exist |
| 5 | Per-directory `.purpose` freshness |
| 6 | Aspect coverage (advisory, non-blocking) |
| 7 | Lore entry expected for significant sessions |
| 8 | Blocking habits not satisfied |
| 9 | Purpose-required patterns from config |
| 10 | Aspect drift detection |
| 11 | Portal gate implementation compliance |
| 12 | Agent permission compliance |

If any blocking check fails, the agent cannot finish until the issue is resolved. This prevents undocumented changes from entering the codebase.

### The Review Pipeline

`paradigm review` runs a two-stage analysis:

**Stage 1 — Compliance**: Checks that Paradigm metadata is complete and consistent.
- Are all modified directories covered by `.purpose` files?
- Do new routes have corresponding `portal.yaml` entries?
- Are aspect anchors still valid?

**Stage 2 — Code Quality**: Analyzes the actual code changes.
- Uses `git diff` to identify what changed
- Checks for common issues (console.log instead of Paradigm logger, missing error handling)
- Validates that commit messages follow conventions

### Running Review in CI

```bash
# In your CI pipeline (GitHub Actions, etc.):
paradigm review --ci
```

The `--ci` flag outputs machine-readable results and sets the exit code based on findings:
- Exit 0: All checks pass
- Exit 1: Blocking issues found

For deeper analysis:
```bash
paradigm review --deep --ci
```

The `--deep` flag adds implementation verification — checking that gates declared in `portal.yaml` are actually implemented in code, and that signals declared in `.purpose` files are actually emitted.

### Git Diff as the Source of Truth

The review pipeline's power comes from `git diff`. Rather than scanning the entire codebase, it focuses on what changed:

```bash
# What review sees:
git diff --name-only HEAD~1   # Which files changed
git diff HEAD~1               # What changed in those files
```

This makes review fast even in large codebases — it only checks what's relevant to the current change.

### Putting It Together: The Full Pipeline

```
Agent makes changes
       |
       v
git add (specific files)
       |
       v
git commit
  |-- pre-commit hook: rebuild scan-index.json
  |-- commit message: type(#symbol): description + Symbols: trailer
       |
       v
git push
       |
       v
CI runs: paradigm review --ci
  |-- Stage 1: compliance checks
  |-- Stage 2: code quality checks
       |
       v
PR review (human)
       |
       v
Merge to main
```

Each layer catches different issues. Pre-commit hooks catch index staleness. The stop hook catches missing documentation. CI review catches compliance and quality issues. Human review catches design and intent issues. Together, they form a defense-in-depth strategy for AI-assisted codebases.

Stop hooks enforce 12 compliance checks at session end
